stories.headline: Assam: The Great Khali extends support to flood-affected people in Nazira
stories.title: Assam: The Great Khali extends support to flood-affected people in Nazira
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
article_sentences: NAZIRA: Internationally acclaimed WWE champion and Indian professional wrestler Dalip Singh Rana, popularly known as ‘The Great Khali,’ has reached out to flood-affected people in Assam during his two-day visit to Sivasagar district.
After participating in a relief-material distribution programme at Dorika Kaibarta village in Sivasagar on Thursday, Khali visited Chumani village in Nazira on Friday.

The programme was organised by True Hope Foundation, Ayan and Deeplina Deka Foundation, which distributed essential items including beds, mattresses, fans, and water filters among flood-affected families.
Khali subsequently visited Tengahola at Bamun Pukhuri, where he participated in an ongoing house-construction initiative undertaken by the three organisations for flood victims.
He inaugurated one newly constructed house at the site.
He also laid the foundation stone for a proposed Hanuman temple to be constructed in the same area under the initiative of True Hope Foundation, Ayan and Deeplina Deka Foundation.

Appreciating the organisations and volunteers involved in rebuilding homes for flood-affected families, Khali said, “Best wishes for this initiative to construct more than 100 houses for flood victims.
May God give greater strength to all the volunteers and organisers so that they can continue serving many more people in society.”
Khali’s visit and participation in the relief and rehabilitation initiatives brought encouragement to the flood-affected families and volunteers engaged in the ongoing reconstruction efforts.

stories.headline: Assam citizens’ forum calls for scientific solution to flood problem
stories.title: Assam citizens’ forum calls for scientific solution to flood problem
stories.summary: The CPI(M) organises ‘demand day’ to seek the national disaster tag for the State’s annual deluge
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
article_sentences: A citizens’ forum in Assam has called for a comprehensive and scientific approach to the flood problem—one that looks beyond temporary relief and embankment repairs and examines the entire river and ecological system.

On Friday (August 21, 2026), members of the Communist Party of India (Marxist) organised ‘demand day’, seeking the national disaster tag for the deluge that leaves scores dead and displaces thousands every year.
The party also demanded ₹20 lakh for the families of those killed in the recent floods, ₹1 lakh in immediate assistance to each affected family and up to ₹10 lakh for houses destroyed in the floods.

The Assam Nagorik Sammilan, a forum headed by academician Hiren Gohain and former Director General of Police Harekrishna Deka, said the State’s geographical position makes it vulnerable to flooding via rivers originating in the mountains of the surrounding hill States.
“It is therefore only natural that construction, mining and other large-scale activities in the upper reaches of these river systems will affect the volume and speed of water flowing into Assam.
And that is precisely where we are witnessing serious changes,” the forum said, citing the recent devastation in Sivasagar, Charaideo, and Jorhat districts.
The forum also warned of a similar disaster if the Eco-Sensitive Zone around Kaziranga National Park and Tiger Reserve is reduced to 1 k.m. from the default 10 km.
“Kaziranga’s Eco-Sensitive Zone cannot be treated as an issue separate from the larger environmental crisis facing Assam.
The conservation of forests, wetlands, and floodplains is closely connected to the State’s ecological security and its ability to cope with floods,” it said.

The forum announced a plan for a convention to bring together environmentalists, forest experts, engineers, river specialists, geologists, historians, social scientists, activists, and people from flood-affected areas to examine the flood and environmental crisis from every possible perspective.

The perspectives include the impact of climate change, changes in river systems, embankments, dams and other infrastructure, mining, deforestation, wetlands, floodplains and the larger development model being followed in the northeast.

stories.headline: Trump loyalist Ed Martin leaves DOJ to focus on election legal battles
stories.title: Trump loyalist Ed Martin leaves DOJ to focus on election legal battles
stories.summary: Ed Martin, a loyal White House ally who held multiple Justice Department posts despite unconventional tactics that sometimes rankled his superiors, is leaving President Donald Trump's administration, the Republican president said Friday. Trump said in a social media post that Martin is leaving his role as the Justice Department's pardon attorney to "fight Legal Battles" surrounding this year's midterm elections and the 2028 presidential election. "I know he will do an outstanding job, ensure Free, Fair, and Honest Elections, and strongly advance our Constitutional Rights," Trump wrote. Martin has been a controversial Trump administration figure since his appointment last year as interim US attorney for the District of Columbia, where he oversaw the dismissal of Jan. 6 cases after Trump's sweeping pardons. Trump later pulled Martin's nomination for the job over bipartisan concerns about his lack of prosecutorial experience and support for rioters who violently attacked the Capitol.

stories.headline: Kashmiriyat in Stone and Deodar
stories.title: Kashmiriyat in Stone and Deodar
stories.summary: The preservation and thoughtful integration of Kashmir’s unique architectural, religious, and historical sites into sustainable eco-tourism hubs is essential for safeguarding the valley’s syncretic cultural ethos. Unlike standard Islamic architecture across the world, Kashmir’s traditional Islamic structures—such as the Khanqah-e-Moula and Jama Masjid—showcase a distinct Vernacular Wooden Architecture, defined by tiered pyramidal roofs (Shikhara-style roofs), heavy deodar woodwork, and intricate papier-mache or Pinjrakari (lattice work). This reflects a seamless fusion of indigenous Kashmiri Buddhist-Hindu stone craftsmanship with Central Asian Sufi motifs. Likewise, early Kashmiri Hindu temples—from the 8th-century Awantipora and Parihaspura ruins and Nara Nag complex to Shankaracharya—utilize grand stone masonry with distinct triangular gables, trefoil arches, and cella-in-water layouts (Kunds), representing a distinct school of ancient architecture unparalleled in continental India. Priority Heritage Sites & Adaptive Tourism Development Khanqah-e-Moula & Shahr-e-Khas (Downtown) are the premier examples of Kashmiri wooden pagoda-style architecture dedicated to Mir Sayyid Ali Hamadani; epicentre of central valley craft culture. Development of heritage walk circuits and restoration of the traditional Zoon Dub (overhanging balconies) and brick facades along the Jhelum riverfront. Integrating river transit (Shikara routes) with guided walking tours will be very much appreciated by everybody including the tourists. Likewise, the Awantipora Ruins, Parihaspura & Naranag Temple Complex are the 8th to 9th-century Utpala and Karkota dynasty stone temples showing distinctive Kashmiri classical architecture of the periods of King Lalitaditya Muktapida. These need to have a restorative look and signages and short movies describing the historic times of the past surrounded by pleasant parks and gardens with an entry fee if found feasible. Hari Parbat Belt (Sharika Temple, Makhdoom Sahib, Gurdwara Chatti Padshahi) The multi-faith hill shrine showcasing Kashmiriyat and Kashmir’s shared spiritual history. Creating continuous pedestrian greenways, herbal gardens, terraced viewpoints, and eco-friendly battery vehicle transportation across the hill complex will be a great teaching history lessons of our mixed culture. These of course will be good revenue earners for the dept. of tourism besides showcasing these historical venues. Rishi Peer (Ali Kadal) is a deeply revered local shrine, and a Rishi-Sufi habitats that represent community-level heritage revered by both Pandits and Muslims. Over the years it seems to have lost its importance with the mass exodus of Pandits. Such places are good examples for Community Restoration. It needs implementation of localized conservation using traditional materials (lime mortar, local stone) paired with neighbourhood green spaces and heritage signage. Ishber and Nishat Belt (Swami Lakshman Joo Ashram & Jeethyar) are centres of Kashmir Shaivism and ancient holy springs (Nagasha) and Goddess Jyshta located along the Dal foothills. These are ideal spots for meditation and developing eco-gardens to preserve the serene environment with quiet reflection zones, native floral landscaping, and digital archives of Kashmiri Shaiva philosophy. Perched atop the adjacent Gopadri Hill on the Zabarwan range, the Shankaracharya Temple stands as a timeless spiritual and historical anchor overlooking Srinagar. Dedicated to Lord Shiva, the stone structure dates back to antiquity, with local traditions attributing its earliest foundations to Jaluka, son of Emperor Ashoka, before being reconstructed by later rulers. The site earned its iconic name after the philosopher Adi Shankaracharya visited Kashmir in the 8th century AD to engage in philosophical debates, meditating at this very spot to revive Advaita Vedanta. Reaching the shrine requires ascending 243 stone steps, rewarding pilgrims and visitors with sweeping panoramic views of Dal Lake and the Jhelum valley—serving as a symbolic precursor to the cultural and scientific intellectualism that later flourished just down the ridge at Pari Mahal. This area needs to build a scenic cable car connecting the Boulevard Road/Dal Lake base to Chashme Shahi, Pari Mahal, and the Shankaracharya foothills to reduce traffic choke points along the winding hill road. An eco-Friendly Shuttle fleet by deploying electric mini-buses to manage hill transport and reduce carbon emissions in the fragile Zabarwan ecosystem. Beyond the manicured terraces of Chashme Shahi, Pari Mahal (the Palace of Fairies) and the associated library ruins of Prince Dara Shikoh represent a pivotal era of Mughal Kashmir, where architectural grandiosity converged with intellectual syncretism. Perched dramatically above Dal Lake, Pari Mahal was constructed in the mid-17th century by Dara Shikoh—the scholar-prince and eldest son of Shah Jahan—not merely as a pleasure garden, but as an observatory, a retreat for Sufi contemplation, and a vibrant centre for the study of astronomy and astrology under his spiritual mentor, Mullah Shah Badakhshi. The site housed a vast library containing priceless manuscripts on comparative religion, Persian translations of the Upanishads (Sirr-i-Akbar), and scientific treatises. Beyond its historic intellectual legacy, Pari Mahal’s heritage value lies in its unique terraced stone architecture, which departs from classic Mughal brick-and-plaster construction in favour of local grey granite masonry adorned with vaulted arches, subterranean chambers, and intricate water channels. Restoring these partially ruined terraces and intellectual halls through rigorous conservation—utilizing lime mortar, localized stone dressing, and timber retrofitting—is crucial for resurrecting their historical identity. To help visitors truly realize the forgotten grandeur of this sanctuary, the site requires context-rich interpretative signages, tactile 3D models of the original six-tiered structure, and QR-enabled digital displays mapping the cosmic and literary pursuits of Dara Shikoh, transforming these evocative ruins into a living centre of Kashmir’s scholastic past. To restore and preserve these invaluable places we need to enforce precise material codes for restoration—prohibiting modern concrete/aluminium cladding in heritage zones like Shahr-e-Khas. Promote traditional earthquake-resistant structural practices such as Dhajji Dewari (timber frame with brick infill) and Taq (timber-laced masonry). By preventing illegal encroachment around historic monuments through marked green belts and strict zoning laws. What we need is craft & culture integration by linking spiritual circuits with local artisanal neighbourhoods (Kani shawl weavers, Papier-mâché experts, copper-smiths, wood carvers), ensuring tourism directly benefits local communities and preserves traditional livelihoods. Providing curated signage, QR-coded audio guides, and localized heritage centres at major hubs to educate visitors on the multi-layered history of the Kashmir valley. Ultimately, the future of Kashmir’s tourism lies not in rapid modernization, but in the meticulous preservation of its physical and spiritual history. By enforcing traditional material codes, protecting the architectural brilliance of both stone and timber, and directly empowering local artisans, the valley can build a sustainable model of eco-tourism. Transforming these priority sites into living heritage hubs does more than secure a steady revenue stream or reduce environmental impact; it revives the fading links of community restoration. Protecting this landscape ensures that the physical remnants of the past—from the grand terraces of Pari Mahal to the quiet sanctuaries of the Sufi-Rishi shrines—continue to stand as a testament to Kashmiriyat, safeguarding the valley’s unique, syncretic cultural ethos for generations to come. Prof Upendra Kaul, Founder Director Gauri Kaul Foundation

stories.headline: Complete erosion of sovereignty as foundation of US-based inter-State system: Iran on US sanctions
stories.title: Complete erosion of sovereignty as foundation of US-based inter-State system: Iran on US sanctions
stories.summary: Iran has condemned new US economic sanctions, accusing Washington of asserting extraterritorial sovereignty over independent nations. Foreign Ministry spokesperson Esmaeil Baqaei said the measures violate international law and warned that combined with a naval blockade, they could erode national sovereignty.
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence

opening: Iran has condemned new US economic sanctions, accusing Washington of asserting extraterritorial sovereignty over independent nations.
Foreign Ministry spokesperson Esmaeil Baqaei said the measures violate international law and warned that combined with a naval blockade, they could erode national sovereignty.
body: Tehran, August 22: Iran on Saturday slammed the latest economic sanctions announced by the United States, calling them arbitrary and saying they have no basis in international law and violate the principle of sovereign equality enshrined in the UN Charter.
The remarks were made by Esmaeil Baqaei, spokesperson for Iran's Ministry of Foreign Affairs, in a post on X on Saturday.
"The United States' declaration of new economic sanctions on Iran is far more than continued unlawful 'economic warfare' against a single country.
It is an assertion of extraterritorial sovereignty over every independent Member State of the United Nations," Baqaei said.

He said no country can lawfully compel foreign banks, enterprises or airports, which are subject to the exclusive jurisdiction of their respective sovereign states, to halt lawful commerce with a third country.
"Such secondary sanctions find no foundation in international law.

They violate the principle of sovereign equality enshrined in Article 2(1) of the UN Charter and breach the customary prohibition on intervention affirmed by the International Court of Justice in the Nicaragua case," he said.
Baqaei further alleged that economic coercion aimed at forcing a sovereign state to alter its lawful policy choices amounts to an internationally wrongful act.

"When combined with a naval blockade amounting to military aggression, these demands reduce the sovereignty of all other States to something provisional, conditional, and revocable at the whim of another power," he said.

He added that compliance with such sanctions does not guarantee immunity or respect, but instead means accepting that banks, enterprises and airports operate "only under a foreign licence." "The end result would be the complete erosion of sovereignty as the foundational basis of the UN-based inter-State system, and a recipe for an abysmal return to full-scale classic colonialism," Baqaei said.
His remarks come after Washington announced a fresh round of sanctions targeting Iran, amid continued tensions between the two countries and broader instability in West Asia.

Trump recently announced what he called the "most crushing economic operation ever taken" against Iran and warned countries providing financial, business or government support to Tehran of "tremendous economic consequences".
The US President said the measures would target Iran's economic lifelines, including oil smuggling networks, financial transfers, exchange houses, ship registries and front companies.
He also called the campaign an "Economic D-Day" and urged American allies to join Washington in isolating Iran.

stories.headline: Supreme Court dismisses PIL petition that challenged death by hanging | Explained
stories.title: Supreme Court dismisses PIL petition that challenged death by hanging | Explained
stories.summary: The central question before the Supreme Court was whether prescribing a single method of execution, hanging, conforms to the constitutional requirement of a procedure that is just, fair and reasonable
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
event term: 'supreme court' in title weight 44
event term: 'supreme court' in summary weight 26.4
article_sentences: The story so far: On August 18, the Supreme Court upheld hanging as the method of executing a death sentence, dismissing a PIL petition challenging its constitutional validity.
The Court held that its earlier decision upholding hanging continues to bind it and found no conclusive scientific evidence to establish that alternatives such as lethal injection are more humane.
The matter was before the Bench of Justice Vikram Nath and Sandeep Mehta.
Why was hanging challenged?

The petitioner challenged the constitutional validity of Section 354(5) of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973, corresponding to Section 393(5) of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023, insofar it prescribes hanging as the sole method of executing a death sentence.
The petition is from 2017.

The central question before the Supreme Court was whether prescribing a single method of execution, hanging, conforms to the constitutional requirement of a procedure that is just, fair and reasonable.
Hanging by the neck was first prescribed as the method of executing a death sentence under the Code of Criminal Procedure.
The long-drop method was intended to cause a fracture of the cervical vertebrae, resulting in an immediate loss of consciousness and death.
The method was premised on a clinical calculation of the height and weight of the condemned.
The issue of whether hanging is a humane method of execution has been examined by various institutions.
The Law Commission of India, in its 35th Report in 1967, examined different modes of execution and acknowledged the view that hanging should be replaced by a more humane and painless method.

The petition is from 2017.

The central question before the Supreme Court was whether prescribing a single method of execution, hanging, conforms to the constitutional requirement of a procedure that is just, fair and reasonable.
Hanging by the neck was first prescribed as the method of executing a death sentence under the Code of Criminal Procedure.
The long-drop method was intended to cause a fracture of the cervical vertebrae, resulting in an immediate loss of consciousness and death.
The method was premised on a clinical calculation of the height and weight of the condemned.
